title: Sentinel-Controlled Loops
learningObjectives: Explain sentinel-controlled loops and their execution flow.
Trace condition checks and state changes across iterations.
Select a suitable loop structure for a given problem.
Identify common termination and boundary mistakes.
Apply the loop pattern in an original small program.

understand.concept: A sentinel is a special input value that ends processing. Check it before treating the value as ordinary data; also handle failed input extraction.
understand.whyItMatters: Sentinel loops handle unknown input counts without requiring a separate length.
understand.explain: Read, check sentinel, process, then read again. Guard empty totals before calculating averages.

examples.title: Sum until -1
examples.explanation: Sentinel is tested before summing; add stream-failure handling for robustness.

examples.title: Count until zero
examples.explanation: Zero ends entry and is not counted.

examples.title: Sentinel with break
examples.explanation: Exit command is not processed as normal data.

examples.title: Extraction-safe condition
examples.explanation: Failed extraction and sentinel both stop processing.

practise.guidedTask: Trace and annotate each of the five Sentinel-Controlled Loops examples. For every iteration, record the relevant variable values, condition result and action. Change one input or bound and predict the new behavior.
practise.independentTask: Write a small C++ program demonstrating sentinel-controlled loops in a practical scenario. Include at least three typical tests, two boundary tests, and one invalid or termination test. Explain how the loop terminates.
hints: Read the first value before processing.
Read the next value at loop end.

questions.explanation: Sentinel signals that input is finished.
No ordinary values means count zero.
